P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

In the equation Zn(s)+2 HCl(aq)→ZnClX2(aq)+HX2(g)\ce{Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g)}Zn(s)+2HCl(aq)​ZnClX2​(aq)+HX2​(g), the symbol (aq) after HCl means that hydrochloric acid is:

state symbols — (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous (Topic 3).

A pure liquid is shown by (l). Mixing up (l) and (aq) is a common slip.
"Aqueous" means dissolved in water.
A gas is shown by (g); (aq) says nothing about bubbling.
State symbols do not show concentration — "dilute" or "concentrated" must be written in words.

Asked: the meaning of (aq).

Concept used: state symbols — (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous (Topic 3).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ A pure liquid is shown by (l). Mixing up (l) and (aq) is a common slip.
    • (b) ✔ "Aqueous" means dissolved in water.
    • (c) ✘ A gas is shown by (g); (aq) says nothing about bubbling.
    • (d) ✘ State symbols do not show concentration — "dilute" or "concentrated" must be written in words.

  2. Answer (b)

P2● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which equation is correctly balanced?

a balanced equation has equal atoms of each element on both sides and correct formulae (box rule, Topic 3).

O is 2 on the left and 1 on the right.
H: 2 × 2 = 4 | 2 × 2 = 4. O: 2 | 2. Formulae are correct.
Oxygen gas is never written as a single O atom.
Atoms match, but HX2OX2\ce{H2O2}HX2​OX2​ is hydrogen peroxide, not water — the formula was changed.

Asked: the correctly balanced equation for forming water.

Concept used: a balanced equation has equal atoms of each element on both sides and correct formulae (box rule, Topic 3).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ O is 2 on the left and 1 on the right.
    • (b) ✔ H: 2 × 2 = 4 | 2 × 2 = 4. O: 2 | 2. Formulae are correct.
    • (c) ✘ Oxygen gas is never written as a single O atom.
    • (d) ✘ Atoms match, but HX2OX2\ce{H2O2}HX2​OX2​ is hydrogen peroxide, not water — the formula was changed.

  2. Answer (b)

P3● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Silver chloride is stored in dark-coloured bottles because:

photolytic decomposition — light can break some compounds apart (Topic 5): 2 AgCl(s)→light2 Ag(s)+ClX2(g)\ce{2AgCl(s) ->[\text{light}] 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g)}2AgCl(s)light​2Ag(s)+ClX2​(g).

Silver chloride is a white solid, not a gas.
Dark glass blocks the light that would decompose it.
It does not react with glass.
The change is one substance breaking up, not combining with oxygen.

Asked: why silver chloride is kept in dark bottles.

Concept used: photolytic decomposition — light can break some compounds apart (Topic 5): 2 AgCl(s)→light2 Ag(s)+ClX2(g)\ce{2AgCl(s) ->[\text{light}] 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g)}2AgCl(s)light​2Ag(s)+ClX2​(g).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Silver chloride is a white solid, not a gas.
    • (b) ✔ Dark glass blocks the light that would decompose it.
    • (c) ✘ It does not react with glass.
    • (d) ✘ The change is one substance breaking up, not combining with oxygen.

  2. Answer (b)

P4● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

In the electrolysis of water, which gas collects at the anode (positive electrode), and how would you test it?

Full solution

Given: electrolysis of water. Asked: the gas at the anode and its test.

Concept used: water splits into hydrogen (at the cathode, −) and oxygen (at the anode, +) (Topic 5). Why it applies: the anode is the positive electrode.

  1. 1

    The anode is the positive electrode, where oxygen is released.

  2. 2

    Oxygen supports burning, so a glowing splint relights (or a burning splint burns more brightly).

  3. Check: the anode tube has the smaller volume — oxygen is half the volume of hydrogen ✔.

  4. Answer Oxygen; a glowing splint relights / a flame burns more brightly.

    Common trap: Giving the "pop" test — that is the test for hydrogen.

P5● FoundationFill in the blank · 1 markOriginal

Fill in the blanks: Oxidation is the ________ of oxygen or the ________ of hydrogen by a substance.

Full solution

Asked: the two missing words.

Concept used: oxidation and reduction are opposites (Topic 7). Why it applies: if you remember reduction = loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen, oxidation is the reverse of both.

  1. 1

    Reduction is loss of oxygen → oxidation is gain of oxygen.

  2. 2

    Reduction is gain of hydrogen → oxidation is loss of hydrogen.

  3. Check: in 2 Cu+OX2→2 CuO\ce{2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO}2Cu+OX2​​2CuO, copper gains oxygen and is oxidised ✔.

  4. Answer gain; loss

    Common trap: Writing "gain; gain". Hydrogen works the opposite way to oxygen.

P6● FoundationTrue/False with justification · 1 markOriginal

True or false? "Rancidity happens because bacteria grow in oily food." Justify.

Full solution

Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils (Topic 7). Why it applies: the statement names the cause of rancidity.

  1. 1

    Rancidity is a chemical change: fats and oils react with oxygen in the air.

  2. 2

    This changes their smell and taste.

  3. 3

    It happens even without germs — which is why nitrogen-flushing (removing oxygen) prevents it.

  4. Check: if germs were the cause, removing oxygen would not help; it does help, so oxygen is the cause ✔.

  5. Answer False. Rancidity is caused by oxidation of fats and oils, not by bacteria.

    Common trap: Mixing up rancidity with food spoilage by microbes.

P7● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

What is the colour of ferrous sulphate crystals, and what is the colour of the solid left after heating them strongly?

Full solution

Given: ferrous sulphate crystals are heated strongly. Asked: colour before and after.

Concept used: thermal decomposition of ferrous sulphate (Topic 5). Why it applies: heating breaks it down into a different solid.

  1. 1

    Hydrated ferrous sulphate, FeSOX4 ⋅ 7 HX2O\ce{FeSO4.7H2O}FeSOX4​⋅7HX2​O, is green.

  2. 2

    Heating first drives off the water of crystallisation.

  3. 3

    Then it decomposes: 2 FeSOX4(s)→heatFeX2OX3(s)+SOX2(g)+SOX3(g)\ce{2FeSO4(s) ->[\text{heat}] Fe2O3(s) + SO2(g) + SO3(g)}2FeSOX4​(s)heat​FeX2​OX3​(s)+SOX2​(g)+SOX3​(g).

  4. 4

    The solid left, ferric oxide (FeX2OX3\ce{Fe2O3}FeX2​OX3​), is reddish-brown.

  5. Check: the equation is balanced (Fe 2 | 2, S 2 | 2, O 8 | 8) and the only solid product is FeX2OX3\ce{Fe2O3}FeX2​OX3​ ✔.

  6. Answer Green → reddish-brown (ferric oxide).

    Common trap: Saying the residue is "white". The crystals turn whitish briefly when they lose water, but the final residue is reddish-brown.

P8● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which of these is a chemical change?

a chemical change forms a new substance that cannot easily be turned back (Topic 1).

Wax sets again on cooling — same substance.
Sugar can be recovered by evaporating the water.
Steam condenses back to water, even though bubbles form.
The runny egg white becomes a firm white solid and cannot be changed back by cooling — a new substance.

Asked: the chemical change.

Concept used: a chemical change forms a new substance that cannot easily be turned back (Topic 1).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Wax sets again on cooling — same substance.
    • (b) ✘ Sugar can be recovered by evaporating the water.
    • (c) ✘ Steam condenses back to water, even though bubbles form.
    • (d) ✔ The runny egg white becomes a firm white solid and cannot be changed back by cooling — a new substance.

  2. Answer (d)

P9● FoundationShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Write a balanced equation, with state symbols, for: "Calcium burns in oxygen to form solid calcium oxide."

Full solution

Given: a word statement. Asked: balanced equation with state symbols.

Concept used: word → formulae → balancing → states (Topic 3). Why it applies: the statement names all reactants, products and the product's state.

  1. 1

    Calcium is a metal → Ca.

  2. 2

    Oxygen gas is diatomic → OX2\ce{O2}OX2​.

  3. 3

    Calcium oxide: Ca (2) and O (2) → simplify → CaO\ce{CaO}CaO.

  4. 4

    Skeletal: Ca+OX2→CaO\ce{Ca + O2 -> CaO}Ca+OX2​​CaO. Count: O 2 | 1.

  5. 5

    Put 2 in front of CaO\ce{CaO}CaO → O 2 | 2; now Ca 1 | 2.

  6. 6

    Put 2 in front of Ca → Ca 2 | 2.

  7. 7

    States: calcium solid (s); oxygen gas (g); calcium oxide solid (s), as stated.

  8. Check: Ca 2 | 2; O 2 | 2 ✔.

  9. Answer 2 Ca(s)+OX2(g)→2 CaO(s)\ce{2Ca(s) + O2(g) -> 2CaO(s)}2Ca(s)+OX2​(g)​2CaO(s)

    Common trap: Writing CaOX2\ce{CaO2}CaOX2​ to "fix" the oxygen. That changes the formula.

P10●● StandardMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which reaction is a displacement reaction?

displacement — a free element pushes another element out of its compound, and that element comes out free (Topic 6).

Two compounds swap ions — double displacement.
Free chlorine takes iodine's place; iodine comes out as a free element.
One reactant breaks down — decomposition.
Two reactants form one product — combination.

Asked: the displacement reaction.

Concept used: displacement — a free element pushes another element out of its compound, and that element comes out free (Topic 6).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Two compounds swap ions — double displacement.
    • (b) ✔ Free chlorine takes iodine's place; iodine comes out as a free element.
    • (c) ✘ One reactant breaks down — decomposition.
    • (d) ✘ Two reactants form one product — combination.

  2. Answer (b)

P11●● StandardMCQ · 1 markOriginal

When Al+HCl→AlClX3+HX2\ce{Al + HCl -> AlCl3 + H2}Al+HCl​AlClX3​+HX2​ is balanced with the smallest whole numbers, the coefficients (in order) are:

hit-and-trial balancing; make odd numbers even by doubling (Topic 3).

H: 3 on the left, 6 on the right.
Matches the working.
Cl: 3 on the left, 6 on the right.
Cl: 6 on the left, 3 on the right.

Asked: the smallest whole-number coefficients.

Concept used: hit-and-trial balancing; make odd numbers even by doubling (Topic 3).

  1. 1

    Working:

    Chlorine: 1 on the left, 3 on the right → try 3 HCl.

  2. 2

    Hydrogen: now 3 (odd) on the left, 2 on the right → double to 6 HCl.

  3. 3

    Hydrogen on the right must be 6 → 3 HX2\ce{H2}HX2​.

  4. 4

    Chlorine on the right must be 6 → 2 AlClX3\ce{AlCl3}AlClX3​.

  5. 5

    Aluminium on the right is 2 → 2 Al.

    2 Al+6 HCl→2 AlClX3+3 HX2\ce{2Al + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2}2Al+6HCl​2AlClX3​+3HX2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    Check: Al 2 | 2; H 6 | 6; Cl 6 | 6 ✔.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ H: 3 on the left, 6 on the right.
    • (b) ✔ Matches the working.
    • (c) ✘ Cl: 3 on the left, 6 on the right.
    • (d) ✘ Cl: 6 on the left, 3 on the right.

  7. Answer (b)

P12●● StandardMCQ · 1 markOriginal

In ZnO+C→Zn+CO\ce{ZnO + C -> Zn + CO}ZnO+C​Zn+CO, the reducing agent is:

the reducing agent removes oxygen from the other substance and is itself oxidised (Topic 7).

ZnO\ce{ZnO}ZnO loses oxygen, so it is reduced — it is the oxidising agent.
Carbon takes oxygen away from ZnO\ce{ZnO}ZnO and is itself oxidised to CO\ce{CO}CO.
, (d) ✘ These are products; agents are always reactants.

Asked: the reducing agent.

Concept used: the reducing agent removes oxygen from the other substance and is itself oxidised (Topic 7).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ ZnO\ce{ZnO}ZnO loses oxygen, so it is reduced — it is the oxidising agent.
    • (b) ✔ Carbon takes oxygen away from ZnO\ce{ZnO}ZnO and is itself oxidised to CO\ce{CO}CO.
    • (c), (d) ✘ These are products; agents are always reactants.

  2. Answer (b)

P13●● StandardAssertion–Reason · 1 markOriginal
AIn the electrolysis of water, the volume of hydrogen collected is twice the volume of oxygen.
RWater contains hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 1 by mass.
the 2 : 1 ratio in water is by number of atoms, not by mass (Topic 5).

Asked: whether A and R are true, and whether R explains A.

Concept used: the 2 : 1 ratio in water is by number of atoms, not by mass (Topic 5).

  1. 1

    A: the volume ratio of HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ to OX2\ce{O2}OX2​ is 2 : 1 → true.

  2. 2

    R: by mass, water has 2 parts hydrogen to 16 parts oxygen, i.e. 1 : 8 → false.

  3. 3

    A true, R false → option (C).

  4. Check: 2 × 1 = 2 (hydrogen) and 1 × 16 = 16 (oxygen) → 2 : 16 = 1 : 8, not 2 : 1 ✔.

  5. Answer (C)

    Common trap: Choosing (A) because "2 : 1" appears in both. Read "by mass" carefully.
P14●● StandardAssertion–Reason · 1 markOriginal
AWhen an iron nail is left in copper sulphate solution, the blue solution becomes pale green.
RIron is more reactive than copper.
displacement by a more reactive metal (Topic 6).

Asked: truth of A and R; does R explain A?

Concept used: displacement by a more reactive metal (Topic 6).

  1. 1

    R is true: iron is above copper on the reactivity ladder.

  2. 2

    Because of R, iron displaces copper: Fe+CuSOX4→FeSOX4+Cu\ce{Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu}Fe+CuSOX4​​FeSOX4​+Cu.

  3. 3

    Blue copper sulphate is replaced by pale green iron(II) sulphate → A is true.

  4. 4

    R is the reason A happens → R explains A.

  5. Check: if iron were less reactive (like silver), there would be no colour change — so R really is the cause ✔.

  6. Answer (A) Both true; R is the correct explanation of A.

P15●● StandardAssertion–Reason · 1 markOriginal
AThe burning of natural gas, CHX4+2 OX2→COX2+2 HX2O\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O}CHX4​+2OX2​​COX2​+2HX2​O, is a combination reaction.
RThe burning of natural gas is an exothermic reaction.
combination needs one product; exothermic means heat is released (Topic 4).

Asked: truth of A and R.

Concept used: combination needs one product; exothermic means heat is released (Topic 4).

  1. 1

    Count the products: COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ and HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O — two → not combination → A is false.

  2. 2

    Burning methane releases heat → R is true.

  3. Check: compare C+OX2→COX2\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}C+OX2​​COX2​ (one product → combination); methane gives two ✔.

  4. Answer (D) A is false but R is true.

    Common trap: Linking "releases heat" with "combination". They describe different things.
P16●● StandardAssertion–Reason · 1 markOriginal
AThe decomposition of silver chloride in sunlight is an endothermic reaction.
REnergy is needed to break the bonds in a compound during decomposition.
most decompositions absorb energy because bond breaking needs energy (Topic 5).

Asked: truth of A and R; does R explain A?

Concept used: most decompositions absorb energy because bond breaking needs energy (Topic 5).

  1. 1

    Silver chloride absorbs light energy to break apart → A is true.

  2. 2

    Bond breaking always needs energy → R is true.

  3. 3

    The energy is absorbed because bonds must be broken → R explains A.

  4. Check: remove the light and the decomposition stops — energy really is being taken in ✔.

  5. Answer (A)

P17●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

LPG contains propane, CX3HX8\ce{C3H8}CX3​HX8​. Balance its burning: CX3HX8+OX2→COX2+HX2O\ce{C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O}CX3​HX8​+OX2​​COX2​+HX2​O.

Full solution

Given: the skeletal equation. Asked: the balanced equation.

Concept used: the fuel rule — balance C first, then H, then O last (Topic 3). Why it applies: oxygen appears on its own as OX2\ce{O2}OX2​, so changing its coefficient cannot upset C or H.

  1. 1

    Carbon: 3 on the left → put 3 in front of COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​.

  2. 2

    Hydrogen: 8 on the left → put 4 in front of HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O (4 × 2 = 8).

  3. 3

    Oxygen on the right: 3 × 2 = 6 (in COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​) + 4 × 1 = 4 (in HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O) = 10.

  4. 4

    Oxygen on the left must be 10 → put 5 in front of OX2\ce{O2}OX2​.

  5. Check: C 3 | 3; H 8 | 8; O 10 | 10 ✔.

  6. Answer CX3HX8+5 OX2→3 COX2+4 HX2O\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}CX3​HX8​+5OX2​​3COX2​+4HX2​O

    Common trap: Balancing O before H — you will then have to redo O.

You got 0 of 1 parts.

P18●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Write the balanced equation with state symbols: "Aluminium reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to give aluminium sulphate solution and hydrogen gas."

Full solution

Given: a word statement with states. Asked: balanced equation with state symbols.

Concept used: criss-cross formulae, then balancing starting from the biggest formula (Topic 2, Topic 3). Why it applies: aluminium sulphate is the most complex formula, so it fixes the other numbers.

  1. 1

    Formulae: Al; HX2SOX4\ce{H2SO4}HX2​SOX4​; aluminium sulphate (Al 3, SOX4\ce{SO4}SOX4​ 2) → AlX2(SOX4)X3\ce{Al2(SO4)3}AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​; HX2\ce{H2}HX2​.

  2. 2

    Start with AlX2(SOX4)X3\ce{Al2(SO4)3}AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​: it has 2 Al → put 2 in front of Al.

  3. 3

    It has 3 sulphate groups → put 3 in front of HX2SOX4\ce{H2SO4}HX2​SOX4​.

  4. 4

    Hydrogen on the left: 3 × 2 = 6 → put 3 in front of HX2\ce{H2}HX2​.

  5. 5

    States: aluminium (s); dilute acid (aq); aluminium sulphate solution (aq); hydrogen gas (g).

  6. Check: Al 2 | 2; H 6 | 6; S 3 | 3; O 12 | 12 ✔.

  7. Answer 2 Al(s)+3 HX2SOX4(aq)→AlX2(SOX4)X3(aq)+3 HX2(g)\ce{2Al(s) + 3H2SO4(aq) -> Al2(SO4)3(aq) + 3H2(g)}2Al(s)+3HX2​SOX4​(aq)​AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​(aq)+3HX2​(g)

    Common trap: Writing AlSOX4\ce{AlSO4}AlSOX4​ — the valencies 3 and 2 must be crossed over.

Tick each part you got right:

You got 0 of 1 parts.

P19●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

A student heats green ferrous sulphate crystals in a boiling tube. (a) Give two observations. (b) Write the balanced equation for the decomposition. (c) Name the type of reaction and explain why the student must point the tube away from others.

Full solution

Given: ferrous sulphate crystals heated in a boiling tube. Asked: observations, equation, type and a safety reason.

Concept used: thermal decomposition (Topic 5). Why it applies: a single compound breaks down on heating.

  1. 1

    (a)

    Water droplets appear on the cooler upper part of the tube (water of crystallisation is driven off).

  2. 2

    The green crystals turn whitish, then a reddish-brown solid is left.

  3. 3

    A smell of burning sulphur is noticed.

    (Any two.)

  4. 4

    (b)

    Write the decomposition: one FeSOX4\ce{FeSO4}FeSOX4​ cannot give whole numbers of FeX2OX3\ce{Fe2O3}FeX2​OX3​, so start with 2 FeSOX4\ce{FeSO4}FeSOX4​.

    2 FeSOX4(s)→heatFeX2OX3(s)+SOX2(g)+SOX3(g)\ce{2FeSO4(s) ->[\text{heat}] Fe2O3(s) + SO2(g) + SO3(g)}2FeSOX4​(s)heat​FeX2​OX3​(s)+SOX2​(g)+SOX3​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    (c)

    One reactant → three products on heating → thermal decomposition.

  6. 6

    The gases SOX2\ce{SO2}SOX2​ and SOX3\ce{SO3}SOX3​ are choking and harmful, and hot material can spurt out, so the mouth must face away from everyone.

  7. Check: Fe 2 | 2; S 2 | 1 + 1 = 2; O 8 | 3 + 2 + 3 = 8 ✔.

  8. Answer (a) any two of the observations above (b) the equation above (c) thermal decomposition; harmful gases and hot spray.

    Common trap: Writing FeSOX4→FeO+SOX3\ce{FeSO4 -> FeO + SO3}FeSOX4​​FeO+SOX3​ — the product is ferric oxide, and two gases are formed.

You got 0 of 3 parts.

P20●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Meera puts a copper wire in silver nitrate solution (test tube 1) and a silver wire in copper sulphate solution (test tube 2). In which tube does a reaction occur? Write its equation and one observation.

Full solution

Given: Cu in AgNOX3\ce{AgNO3}AgNOX3​; Ag in CuSOX4\ce{CuSO4}CuSOX4​. Asked: which reacts, the equation, one observation.

Concept used: a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one; not the other way round (Topic 6). Why it applies: each tube pairs a free metal with a compound of another metal.

  1. 1

    On the reactivity ladder, copper is above silver → copper is more reactive.

  2. 2

    Tube 1: copper can displace silver → a reaction occurs.

  3. 3

    Copper forms copper(II) nitrate, Cu(NOX3)X2\ce{Cu(NO3)2}Cu(NOX3​)X2​; silver is set free.

  4. 4

    Balance nitrate (2 needed) → 2 AgNOX3\ce{2AgNO3}2AgNOX3​, then silver → 2 Ag\ce{2Ag}2Ag.

    Cu(s)+2 AgNOX3(aq)→Cu(NOX3)X2(aq)+2 Ag(s)\ce{Cu(s) + 2AgNO3(aq) -> Cu(NO3)2(aq) + 2Ag(s)}Cu(s)+2AgNOX3​(aq)​Cu(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+2Ag(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Tube 2: silver is less reactive than copper → it cannot displace copper → no reaction.

  6. 6

    Observation in tube 1: a shiny greyish-white layer of silver forms on the wire, and the colourless solution slowly turns blue (copper nitrate is blue).

  7. Check: Cu 1 | 1; Ag 2 | 2; N 2 | 2; O 6 | 6 ✔.

  8. Answer Test tube 1 only; equation and observation as above.

    Common trap: Writing an equation for tube 2 just because two substances are given.

P21●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Sodium carbonate solution is added to calcium chloride solution and a white solid forms. Write the balanced equation with state symbols and classify the reaction in two ways, giving reasons.

Full solution

Given: two solutions mixed; a white solid forms. Asked: balanced equation with states; two classifications.

Concept used: double displacement and precipitation (Topic 6). Why it applies: two compounds in solution swap partners and an insoluble product appears.

  1. 1

    Swap partners: Ca joins COX3\ce{CO3}COX3​ → CaCOX3\ce{CaCO3}CaCOX3​; Na joins Cl → NaCl\ce{NaCl}NaCl.

  2. 2

    Skeletal: NaX2COX3+CaClX2→CaCOX3+NaCl\ce{Na2CO3 + CaCl2 -> CaCO3 + NaCl}NaX2​COX3​+CaClX2​​CaCOX3​+NaCl. Na 2 | 1; Cl 2 | 1.

  3. 3

    Put 2 in front of NaCl\ce{NaCl}NaCl → Na 2 | 2 and Cl 2 | 2.

  4. 4

    States: the white solid is calcium carbonate (s); the rest are solutions (aq).

  5. 5

    Both reactants are compounds exchanging ions → double displacement.

  6. 6

    An insoluble solid forms → precipitation.

  7. Check: Na 2 | 2; C 1 | 1; O 3 | 3; Ca 1 | 1; Cl 2 | 2 ✔.

  8. Answer NaX2COX3(aq)+CaClX2(aq)→CaCOX3(s)+2 NaCl(aq)\ce{Na2CO3(aq) + CaCl2(aq) -> CaCO3(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}NaX2​COX3​(aq)+CaClX2​(aq)​CaCOX3​(s)+2NaCl(aq) — double displacement and precipitation.

    Common trap: Marking NaCl\ce{NaCl}NaCl as the precipitate. Sodium chloride is soluble; calcium carbonate is not.

P22●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

During a reaction in a test tube, your palm holding the tube feels cold. (a) Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? (b) Explain using the direction of heat flow.

Full solution

Given: the tube feels cold. Asked: exo or endo, with a heat-flow reason.

Concept used: heat flows from warmer to cooler; a reaction that takes heat in is endothermic (Topic 5). Why it applies: your palm is the warmer object.

  1. 1

    Heat always flows from a warmer object to a cooler one.

  2. 2

    Your palm feels cold because heat is flowing out of your hand into the tube.

  3. 3

    So the reaction mixture is absorbing heat from its surroundings.

  4. 4

    A reaction that absorbs energy is endothermic.

  5. Check: the opposite case (quicklime + water) makes the hand feel hot, and that reaction is exothermic — consistent ✔.

  6. Answer (a) Endothermic. (b) Heat flows from your hand into the reaction mixture, which absorbs it.

    Common trap: "The tube gives coldness to my hand." Cold does not flow — heat leaves your hand.

P23●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

(a) A silver anklet turns black and a copper vessel turns green over time. Name the process and the substances formed. (b) Suggest two ways to protect an iron gate from the same kind of damage.

Full solution

Given: blackened silver, green copper. Asked: the process, the substances, two ways to protect iron.

Concept used: corrosion — metals damaged by substances in the air (Topic 7). Why it applies: both metals change only on their surface, over time, in air.

  1. 1

    The process is corrosion.

  2. 2

    Silver reacts with sulphur compounds (mainly hydrogen sulphide) in the air → black silver sulphide, AgX2S\ce{Ag2S}AgX2​S.

  3. 3

    Copper reacts slowly with moist carbon dioxide and oxygen → green basic copper carbonate.

  4. 4

    Iron corrodes (rusts) when air and moisture reach it, so protection must keep them out.

  5. 5

    Two ways: paint it; apply oil or grease; or galvanise it (coat with zinc).

  6. Check: each protection method works by putting a barrier between the iron and air/moisture ✔.

  7. Answer (a) Corrosion; silver sulphide (black) and basic copper carbonate (green). (b) Any two: paint, oil/grease, galvanising.

    Common trap: Calling the black coating on silver "rust". Rust is the name for iron's corrosion only.

You got 0 of 2 parts.

P24●● StandardLong answer · 5 marksOriginal

Write balanced equations for the following and name the type of each reaction:
(i) heating lead nitrate; (ii) magnesium ribbon in copper sulphate solution; (iii) ammonia gas meets hydrogen chloride gas; (iv) potassium iodide solution added to lead nitrate solution; (v) hydrogen passed over heated copper(II) oxide.

Full solution

Given: five reactions in words. Asked: balanced equation and type for each.

Concept used: balancing (Topic 3) and the "Which type is it?" routine (wrap-up). Why it applies: each reaction must be written, then classified by its pattern.

  1. 1

    (i) Heating lead nitrate

    One reactant breaks into lead oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.

  2. 2

    Balancing needs 2 Pb(NOX3)X2\ce{Pb(NO3)2}Pb(NOX3​)X2​ to give whole numbers (Topic 3 worked example 9).

    2 Pb(NOX3)X2(s)→heat2 PbO(s)+4 NOX2(g)+OX2(g)\ce{2Pb(NO3)2(s) ->[\text{heat}] 2PbO(s) + 4NO2(g) + O2(g)}2Pb(NOX3​)X2​(s)heat​2PbO(s)+4NOX2​(g)+OX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    One reactant → three products on heating → thermal decomposition.

  4. 1

    (ii) Magnesium in copper sulphate

    Magnesium is above copper → it displaces copper.

    Mg(s)+CuSOX4(aq)→MgSOX4(aq)+Cu(s)\ce{Mg(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> MgSO4(aq) + Cu(s)}Mg(s)+CuSOX4​(aq)​MgSOX4​(aq)+Cu(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 2

    Free Mg in, free Cu out → displacement.

  6. 1

    (iii) Ammonia + hydrogen chloride

    The two gases join into white ammonium chloride.

    NHX3(g)+HCl(g)→NHX4Cl(s)\ce{NH3(g) + HCl(g) -> NH4Cl(s)}NHX3​(g)+HCl(g)​NHX4​Cl(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 2

    Two reactants → one product → combination.

  8. 1

    (iv) Potassium iodide + lead nitrate

    Ions swap: lead with iodide, potassium with nitrate.

    Pb(NOX3)X2(aq)+2 KI(aq)→PbIX2(s)+2 KNOX3(aq)\ce{Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)}Pb(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+2KI(aq)​PbIX2​(s)+2KNOX3​(aq)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 2

    Two compounds exchange ions; yellow solid forms → double displacement and precipitation.

  10. 1

    (v) Hydrogen over heated copper(II) oxide

    Hydrogen removes the oxygen from copper oxide.

    CuO(s)+HX2(g)→heatCu(s)+HX2O(l)\ce{CuO(s) + H2(g) ->[\text{heat}] Cu(s) + H2O(l)}CuO(s)+HX2​(g)heat​Cu(s)+HX2​O(l)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 2

    CuO\ce{CuO}CuO loses oxygen (reduced); HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ gains oxygen (oxidised) → redox. Free HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ in, free Cu out → also displacement.

  12. Check: (i) Pb 2 | 2, N 4 | 4, O 12 | 2 + 8 + 2 = 12. (ii) Mg, Cu, S 1 | 1; O 4 | 4. (iii) N 1 | 1, H 4 | 4, Cl 1 | 1. (iv) Pb 1 | 1, N 2 | 2, O 6 | 6, K 2 | 2, I 2 | 2. (v) Cu 1 | 1, O 1 | 1, H 2 | 2 ✔.

  13. Answer The five equations and types above. Marking guide: 1 mark per part — ½ for the balanced equation, ½ for the correct type.

    Common trap: In (v), writing "copper is reduced". Copper oxide is the substance reduced.

P31●● StandardDiagram-based · 3 marksOriginal

Diagram: heating ferrous sulphate crystals the correct way

(a) Draw a labelled diagram showing the correct way to heat ferrous sulphate crystals in a boiling tube. (b) State two safety points shown in your diagram. (c) How should you smell the gas given off?

Full solution

Given: the CBSE practical "action of heat on ferrous sulphate crystals". Asked: a labelled diagram, two safety points, and the correct way to smell.

Concept used: thermal decomposition gives off harmful gases (SOX2\ce{SO2}SOX2​, SOX3\ce{SO3}SOX3​), so the set-up must keep the tube's mouth and its gases away from people (see the diagram in Topic 5). Why it applies: every safety feature in the diagram follows from that one danger.

  1. 1

    (a) What to draw

    Draw a burner / spirit lamp with a flame.

  2. 2

    Draw a boiling tube held at an angle of about 45° over the flame.

  3. 3

    Show a test-tube holder (or tongs) gripping the tube near its mouth.

  4. 4

    Show green ferrous sulphate crystals at the bottom of the tube.

  5. 5

    Point the mouth of the tube away from you (add an arrow: "mouth pointing away").

  6. 6

    Optional: water droplets near the cooler upper part; a small label "SOX2\ce{SO2}SOX2​ + SOX3\ce{SO3}SOX3​ gases".

    Labels required: boiling tube, test-tube holder, ferrous sulphate crystals, burner (flame).

    (b) Two safety points (any two)

  7. 7

    The tube is held with a holder, not by hand, because it gets very hot.

  8. 8

    The mouth points away from you and others, because harmful gases and hot material can come out.

  9. 9

    The tube is tilted, so heat is spread and the crystals do not spurt out suddenly.

  10. 10

    (c) Smelling the gas

    Do not put your nose to the tube.

  11. 11

    Hold the tube away and waft (fan) the air from its mouth towards your nose with your hand.

  12. Check: every label in the list appears in the NCERT activity and in the Topic 5 diagram ✔.

  13. Answer A labelled diagram with tube, holder, crystals and burner, mouth pointing away; any two safety points; smell by wafting.

    Marking guide: (a) diagram 1 (½ for a tilted tube in a holder over a flame, ½ for labels); (b) 1 (½ each); (c) 1.
    Common trap: Drawing the tube upright with its mouth towards the student, or showing the student sniffing directly.

P25●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: Rohan's electrolysis log

Rohan set up the electrolysis of water with a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid. He recorded the gas volumes in the two inverted tubes:

Time (min) Tube P (mL) Tube Q (mL)
2 4.0 2.0
4 8.2 4.0
6 12.0 6.1
8 ? 8.0

(a) Which tube is over the cathode? Name the gas in it. (1)
(b) Predict the volume in tube P at 8 minutes. Show your working. (1)
(c) Rohan first tried with distilled water only and almost no bubbles formed. Why? (1)
(d) Write the balanced equation and name the type of reaction. (1)

Full solution

Given: volume readings for tubes P and Q. Asked: parts (a)–(d).

Concept used: electrolysis of water gives hydrogen (cathode) and oxygen (anode) in a 2 : 1 volume ratio; pure water conducts poorly (Topic 5). Why it applies: the data show a steady 2 : 1 pattern.

  1. 1

    (a)

    At every time, tube P has about twice the gas of tube Q.

  2. 2

    Hydrogen is produced in double the volume, at the cathode.

  3. 3

    So tube P is over the cathode; the gas is hydrogen.

  4. 4

    (b)

    Ratio P : Q = 2 : 1.

  5. 5

    At 8 min, Q = 8.0 mL.

    P=2×8.0 mL\text{P} = 2 \times 8.0\ \text{mL}P=2×8.0 mLSwipe to see the whole equation →
    P=16.0 mL\text{P} = 16.0\ \text{mL}P=16.0 mLSwipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    (c)

    Distilled water has almost no ions to carry current, so it is a very poor conductor.

  7. 7

    Without current, electrolysis cannot happen. The acid supplies ions.

  8. 8

    (d)

    2 HX2O(l)→electric current2 HX2(g)+OX2(g)\ce{2H2O(l) ->[\text{electric current}] 2H2(g) + O2(g)}2HX2​O(l)electric current​2HX2​(g)+OX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  9. 9

    One compound broken down by electricity → electrolytic decomposition (endothermic).

  10. Check: 16.0 continues the steady rise in P of about 2 mL per minute (12.0 at 6 min) ✔; equation H 4 | 4, O 2 | 2 ✔.

  11. Answer (a) P, hydrogen (b) about 16 mL (c) distilled water is a poor conductor (d) equation above; electrolytic decomposition.

    Common trap: Thinking small differences (8.2 instead of 8.0) break the rule — real measurements have small errors; the pattern is still 2 : 1.

P26●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: Welding railway tracks

On Indian Railways, gaps between rail sections are often joined on site by thermit welding. A mixture of iron(III) oxide powder and aluminium powder is lit in a mould over the joint. The reaction gives off so much heat that the iron formed is molten, and it flows into the gap and joins the rails.

FeX2OX3(s)+2 Al(s)→AlX2OX3(s)+2 Fe(l)+heat\ce{Fe2O3(s) + 2Al(s) -> Al2O3(s) + 2Fe(l)} + \text{heat}FeX2​OX3​(s)+2Al(s)​AlX2​OX3​(s)+2Fe(l)+heatSwipe to see the whole equation →

(a) Is this a displacement or a double displacement reaction? Give a reason. (1)
(b) Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced. (1)
(c) Why does the iron come out as a liquid? (1)
(d) Would the reaction work if copper powder were used instead of aluminium? Explain. (1)

Full solution

Given: the thermit reaction and its use. Asked: parts (a)–(d).

Concept used: displacement by a more reactive metal; redox by gain/loss of oxygen; exothermic reactions (Topic 4, Topic 6, Topic 7). Why it applies: aluminium takes oxygen away from iron oxide and a lot of heat is released.

  1. 1

    (a)

    A free element, aluminium, reacts with a compound, and iron comes out free → displacement.

  2. 2

    (b)

    Al becomes AlX2OX3\ce{Al2O3}AlX2​OX3​: aluminium gains oxygen → aluminium is oxidised.

  3. 3

    FeX2OX3\ce{Fe2O3}FeX2​OX3​ becomes Fe: iron(III) oxide loses oxygen → iron(III) oxide is reduced.

  4. 4

    (c)

    The reaction is highly exothermic.

  5. 5

    The heat raises the iron above its melting point (about 1538 °C), so it forms as a liquid.

  6. 6

    (d)

    Copper is less reactive than iron (lower on the ladder).

  7. 7

    So copper cannot displace iron from iron oxide → no.

  8. Check: Fe 2 | 2; O 3 | 3; Al 2 | 2 ✔.

  9. Answer (a) displacement (b) Al oxidised, FeX2OX3\ce{Fe2O3}FeX2​OX3​ reduced (c) highly exothermic (d) no — copper is less reactive than iron.

    Common trap: In (b), writing "iron is reduced". Iron is the product; iron(III) oxide was reduced.

P27●●● AdvancedLong answer · 5 marksOriginal

Identify X, Y and Z

A white solid X is heated strongly. It gives a white solid Y and a gas that turns lime water milky. When water is added to Y, the mixture becomes very hot and forms Z. A solution of Z is used for whitewashing walls.
(a) Identify X, Y and Z with formulae. (b) Write balanced equations for both reactions, with state symbols. (c) Classify each reaction in two ways.

Full solution

Given: clues about X, Y, Z and a gas. Asked: identities, equations, classifications.

Concept used: work backwards from the clues you recognise (Topic 4, Topic 5). Why it applies: two clues — "turns lime water milky" and "whitewashing" — point to known substances.

  1. 1

    A gas that turns lime water milky is carbon dioxide.

  2. 2

    A solution used for whitewashing is slaked lime, calcium hydroxide → Z = Ca(OH)X2\ce{Ca(OH)2}Ca(OH)X2​.

  3. 3

    Z forms from Y + water with a lot of heat → Y is quicklime, calcium oxide, CaO\ce{CaO}CaO.

  4. 4

    X gives CaO\ce{CaO}CaO and COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ on heating → X is calcium carbonate, CaCOX3\ce{CaCO3}CaCOX3​.

  5. 5

    Reaction 1:

    CaCOX3(s)→heatCaO(s)+COX2(g)\ce{CaCO3(s) ->[\text{heat}] CaO(s) + CO2(g)}CaCOX3​(s)heat​CaO(s)+COX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    One reactant → two products, needs heating → thermal decomposition, endothermic.

  7. 7

    Reaction 2:

    CaO(s)+HX2O(l)→Ca(OH)X2(aq)+heat\ce{CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq)} + \text{heat}CaO(s)+HX2​O(l)​Ca(OH)X2​(aq)+heatSwipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    Two reactants → one product, heat given out → combination, exothermic.

  9. Check: Reaction 1: Ca 1 | 1, C 1 | 1, O 3 | 3. Reaction 2: Ca 1 | 1, O 2 | 2, H 2 | 2 ✔. All clues are explained ✔.

  10. Answer (a) X = CaCOX3\ce{CaCO3}CaCOX3​, Y = CaO\ce{CaO}CaO, Z = Ca(OH)X2\ce{Ca(OH)2}Ca(OH)X2​ (b) the two equations above (c) Reaction 1: thermal decomposition, endothermic; Reaction 2: combination, exothermic.

    Marking guide: (a) 1½ (½ each); (b) 2 (1 each, with states); (c) 1½.
    Common trap: Swapping Y and Z — quicklime (CaO\ce{CaO}CaO) comes before water is added; slaked lime (Ca(OH)X2\ce{Ca(OH)2}Ca(OH)X2​) after.

P28●●● AdvancedShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Hydrogen sulphide and sulphur dioxide react to give yellow sulphur: 2 HX2S+SOX2→3 S+2 HX2O\ce{2H2S + SO2 -> 3S + 2H2O}2HX2​S+SOX2​​3S+2HX2​O. Aman says: "Nothing is oxidised here, because no substance gains oxygen." Is he right? Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced.

Full solution

Given: the balanced equation and Aman's claim. Asked: evaluate the claim; name oxidised and reduced substances.

Concept used: oxidation also means loss of hydrogen (Topic 7). Why it applies: one reactant here contains hydrogen and loses it.

  1. 1

    SOX2\ce{SO2}SOX2​ becomes S: it loses oxygen → SOX2\ce{SO2}SOX2​ is reduced.

  2. 2

    HX2S\ce{H2S}HX2​S becomes S: it loses hydrogen → HX2S\ce{H2S}HX2​S is oxidised.

  3. 3

    The oxygen from SOX2\ce{SO2}SOX2​ and the hydrogen from HX2S\ce{H2S}HX2​S join to form water.

  4. 4

    So oxidation does happen — by loss of hydrogen — and Aman is wrong.

  5. Check: H 4 | 4; S 3 | 3; O 2 | 2 ✔; and we found one oxidation and one reduction, as every redox reaction needs ✔.

  6. Answer Aman is wrong. HX2S\ce{H2S}HX2​S is oxidised; SOX2\ce{SO2}SOX2​ is reduced.

    Common trap: Using only the oxygen definition and missing the hydrogen definition.

P29●●● AdvancedShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Two students balance the decomposition KClOX3→KCl+OX2\ce{KClO3 -> KCl + O2}KClOX3​​KCl+OX2​.

  • Riya writes: KClOX3→KCl+OX3\ce{KClO3 -> KCl + O3}KClOX3​​KCl+OX3​
  • Arjun writes: 2 KClOX3→2 KCl+3 OX2\ce{2KClO3 -> 2KCl + 3O2}2KClOX3​​2KCl+3OX2​

Who is correct? Explain what is wrong with the other answer.

Full solution

Given: two attempted answers. Asked: which is correct and why.

Concept used: a balanced equation needs equal atoms and unchanged formulae — the box rule (Topic 3). Why it applies: one student changed a formula.

  1. 1

    Check Arjun's atoms: K 2 | 2; Cl 2 | 2; O 6 | 3 × 2 = 6 ✔.

  2. 2

    Check Arjun's formulae: unchanged — only coefficients were added ✔.

  3. 3

    Check Riya's atoms: K 1 | 1, Cl 1 | 1, O 3 | 3 — they match.

  4. 4

    Check Riya's formulae: she changed OX2\ce{O2}OX2​ to OX3\ce{O3}OX3​, which is ozone, a different substance. The gas formed is oxygen, OX2\ce{O2}OX2​.

  5. Check: Arjun's coefficients 2, 2, 3 have no common factor, so they are the smallest whole numbers ✔.

  6. Answer Arjun is correct. Riya broke the box rule — her equation describes a reaction that does not happen.

    Common trap: Accepting any equation whose atoms add up. The formulae must also be correct.

Concept used: read the ratio from the balanced equation 2 HX2O→2 HX2+OX2\ce{2H2O -> 2H2 + O2}2HX2​O​2HX2​+OX2​ (Topic 5).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Ignores the formula HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O.
    • (b) ✔ 2 molecules of HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ per 1 molecule of OX2\ce{O2}OX2​.
    • (c) ✘ Compares 4 H atoms with 1 O₂ molecule.
    • (d) ✘ Reverses the ratio.

  2. Answer (b)

    (The Exemplar says "mole ratio"; moles are a Class 11 idea — here it simply means the ratio of molecules.)

E8●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch1 SA 21

Fill in x and y: (a) Pb(NOX3)X2(aq)+2 KI(aq)→PbIX2(x)+2 KNOX3(y)\ce{Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq)} \rightarrow \ce{PbI2}(x) + \ce{2KNO3}(y)Pb(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+2KI(aq)→PbIX2​(x)+2KNOX3​(y) (b) Cu(s)+2 AgNOX3(aq)→Cu(NOX3)X2(aq)+x(s)\ce{Cu(s) + 2AgNO3(aq)} \rightarrow \ce{Cu(NO3)2(aq)} + x(\text{s})Cu(s)+2AgNOX3​(aq)→Cu(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+x(s) (c) Zn(s)+HX2SOX4(aq)→ZnSOX4(x)+HX2(y)\ce{Zn(s) + H2SO4(aq)} \rightarrow \ce{ZnSO4}(x) + \ce{H2}(y)Zn(s)+HX2​SOX4​(aq)→ZnSOX4​(x)+HX2​(y) (d) CaCOX3(s)→  x  CaO(s)+COX2(g)\ce{CaCO3(s)} \xrightarrow{\;x\;} \ce{CaO(s) + CO2(g)}CaCOX3​(s)x​CaO(s)+COX2​(g)

Full solution

Given: four equations with gaps. Asked: x and y.

Concept used: state symbols, balancing and reaction conditions (Topic 3, Topic 5, Topic 6). Why it applies: each gap is either a state, a missing product or a condition.

  1. 1

    (a) Lead iodide is the yellow precipitate → x = (s).

  2. 2

    (a) Potassium nitrate stays dissolved → y = (aq).

  3. 3

    (b) Copper displaces silver; the left has 2 Ag, so the right needs 2Ag → x = 2Ag.

  4. 4

    (c) Zinc sulphate stays dissolved → x = (aq).

  5. 5

    (c) Hydrogen is a gas → y = (g).

  6. 6

    (d) Calcium carbonate breaks down when heated → x = heat.

  7. Check: with x = 2Ag, equation (b) is balanced: Cu 1 | 1, Ag 2 | 2, N 2 | 2, O 6 | 6 ✔.

  8. Answer (a) x = (s), y = (aq) (b) x = 2Ag (c) x = (aq), y = (g) (d) x = heat.

    Common trap: In (b), writing just "Ag" — the coefficient 2 is needed to balance silver.

E9●●● AdvancedShort answer · 4 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch1 SA 23

Identify the reducing agent: (a) 4 NHX3+5 OX2→4 NO+6 HX2O\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O}4NHX3​+5OX2​​4NO+6HX2​O (b) HX2O+FX2→HF+HOF\ce{H2O + F2 -> HF + HOF}HX2​O+FX2​​HF+HOF (c) FeX2OX3+3 CO→2 Fe+3 COX2\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}FeX2​OX3​+3CO​2Fe+3COX2​ (d) 2 HX2+OX2→2 HX2O\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}2HX2​+OX2​​2HX2​O

Full solution

Given: four balanced equations. Asked: the reducing agent in each.

Concept used: the reducing agent is the substance oxidised — it gains oxygen or loses hydrogen (Topic 7). Why it applies: in each reaction exactly one reactant gains oxygen or loses hydrogen.

  1. 1

    (a) NHX3\ce{NH3}NHX3​ → NO\ce{NO}NO: ammonia loses hydrogen and gains oxygen → oxidised → reducing agent: NHX3\ce{NH3}NHX3​.

  2. 2

    (b) HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O → HOF\ce{HOF}HOF: water loses one hydrogen (to fluorine) → oxidised → reducing agent: HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O. (Fluorine gains hydrogen → reduced.)

  3. 3

    (c) CO\ce{CO}CO → COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​: carbon monoxide gains oxygen → reducing agent: CO\ce{CO}CO.

  4. 4

    (d) HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ → HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O: hydrogen gains oxygen → reducing agent: HX2\ce{H2}HX2​.

  5. Check (balance): (a) N 4 | 4, H 12 | 12, O 10 | 10 ✔; (b) H 2 | 2, O 1 | 1, F 2 | 2 ✔; (c) Fe 2 | 2, O 6 | 6, C 3 | 3 ✔; (d) H 4 | 4, O 2 | 2 ✔.

  6. Answer (a) NHX3\ce{NH3}NHX3​ (b) HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O (c) CO\ce{CO}CO (d) HX2\ce{H2}HX2​

    Common trap: In (b), choosing FX2\ce{F2}FX2​ because "it's the reactive one". Fluorine is the oxidising agent — it gains hydrogen and is reduced.

E10●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch1 SA 35 (a)–(f)

Balance and classify: (a) Mg+ClX2→MgClX2\ce{Mg + Cl2 -> MgCl2}Mg+ClX2​​MgClX2​ (b) HgO→heatHg+OX2\ce{HgO ->[\text{heat}] Hg + O2}HgOheat​Hg+OX2​ (c) Na+S→fuseNaX2S\ce{Na + S ->[\text{fuse}] Na2S}Na+Sfuse​NaX2​S (d) TiClX4+Mg→Ti+MgClX2\ce{TiCl4 + Mg -> Ti + MgCl2}TiClX4​+Mg​Ti+MgClX2​ (e) CaO+SiOX2→CaSiOX3\ce{CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3}CaO+SiOX2​​CaSiOX3​ (f) HX2OX2→UV lightHX2O+OX2\ce{H2O2 ->[\text{UV light}] H2O + O2}HX2​OX2​UV light​HX2​O+OX2​

Full solution

Given: six skeletal equations. Asked: balance and classify each.

Concept used: hit-and-trial balancing (Topic 3) and the "Which type is it?" routine (wrap-up). Why it applies: each must be balanced before its pattern is read.

  1. 1

    (a)

    Count: Mg 1 | 1; Cl 2 | 2 → already balanced.

  2. 2

    Two reactants → one product → combination.

    Mg(s)+ClX2(g)→MgClX2(s)\ce{Mg(s) + Cl2(g) -> MgCl2(s)}Mg(s)+ClX2​(g)​MgClX2​(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 1

    (b)

    Oxygen: 1 on the left, 2 on the right → put 2 in front of HgO\ce{HgO}HgO.

  4. 2

    Mercury: now 2 on the left → put 2 in front of Hg.

  5. 3

    One reactant → two products on heating → thermal decomposition.

    2 HgO(s)→heat2 Hg(l)+OX2(g)\ce{2HgO(s) ->[\text{heat}] 2Hg(l) + O2(g)}2HgO(s)heat​2Hg(l)+OX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 1

    (c)

    Sodium: 1 on the left, 2 on the right → put 2 in front of Na.

  7. 2

    Two reactants → one product → combination.

    2 Na(s)+S(s)→fuseNaX2S(s)\ce{2Na(s) + S(s) ->[\text{fuse}] Na2S(s)}2Na(s)+S(s)fuse​NaX2​S(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 1

    (d)

    Chlorine: 4 on the left, 2 on the right → put 2 in front of MgClX2\ce{MgCl2}MgClX2​.

  9. 2

    Magnesium: now 2 on the right → put 2 in front of Mg.

  10. 3

    Free Mg takes titanium's place; Ti comes out free → displacement (Mg is more reactive than Ti).

    TiClX4(l)+2 Mg(s)→Ti(s)+2 MgClX2(s)\ce{TiCl4(l) + 2Mg(s) -> Ti(s) + 2MgCl2(s)}TiClX4​(l)+2Mg(s)​Ti(s)+2MgClX2​(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 1

    (e)

    Count: Ca 1 | 1; Si 1 | 1; O 1 + 2 = 3 | 3 → already balanced.

  12. 2

    Two reactants → one product → combination.

    CaO(s)+SiOX2(s)→CaSiOX3(s)\ce{CaO(s) + SiO2(s) -> CaSiO3(s)}CaO(s)+SiOX2​(s)​CaSiOX3​(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 1

    (f)

    Oxygen: 2 on the left; 1 + 2 = 3 on the right (odd) → put 2 in front of HX2OX2\ce{H2O2}HX2​OX2​ (O on the left = 4).

  14. 2

    Hydrogen: now 4 on the left → put 2 in front of HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O (O on the right = 2 + 2 = 4).

  15. 3

    One reactant → two products, driven by UV light → photolytic decomposition.

    2 HX2OX2(l)→UV light2 HX2O(l)+OX2(g)\ce{2H2O2(l) ->[\text{UV light}] 2H2O(l) + O2(g)}2HX2​OX2​(l)UV light​2HX2​O(l)+OX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  16. Check: (b) Hg 2 | 2, O 2 | 2; (c) Na 2 | 2, S 1 | 1; (d) Ti 1 | 1, Cl 4 | 4, Mg 2 | 2; (f) H 4 | 4, O 4 | 4 ✔.

  17. Answer (a) combination (b) thermal decomposition (c) combination (d) displacement (e) combination (f) photolytic decomposition — with the balanced equations above.

    Common trap: In (a) and (e), adding coefficients to equations that are already balanced.

E11●●● AdvancedLong answer · 5 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch1 LA 39

Blue copper(II) nitrate powder is heated; it gives black copper oxide, oxygen and a brown gas X. (a) Balanced equation (b) Identify X (c) Type of reaction (d) pH range of a solution of X in water.

Full solution

Given: heating copper(II) nitrate gives CuO, OX2\ce{O2}OX2​ and a brown gas. Asked: (a)–(d).

Concept used: thermal decomposition of a nitrate, like lead nitrate in Topic 5; balancing with odd/even oxygen. Why it applies: metal nitrates give the oxide, brown nitrogen dioxide and oxygen on heating.

  1. 1

    The brown gas from a heated nitrate is nitrogen dioxide, NOX2\ce{NO2}NOX2​.

  2. 2

    Skeletal: Cu(NOX3)X2→CuO+NOX2+OX2\ce{Cu(NO3)2 -> CuO + NO2 + O2}Cu(NOX3​)X2​​CuO+NOX2​+OX2​.

  3. 3

    Nitrogen: 2 on the left → put 2 in front of NOX2\ce{NO2}NOX2​.

  4. 4

    Oxygen: 6 on the left; 1 + 4 + 2 = 7 on the right → one too many; we cannot use half an OX2\ce{O2}OX2​.

  5. 5

    Double the nitrate: 2 Cu(NOX3)X2\ce{2Cu(NO3)2}2Cu(NOX3​)X2​ → Cu 2, N 4, O 12 on the left.

  6. 6

    Copper: put 2 in front of CuO\ce{CuO}CuO. Nitrogen: put 4 in front of NOX2\ce{NO2}NOX2​.

  7. 7

    Oxygen on the right: 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 ✔.

    2 Cu(NOX3)X2(s)→heat2 CuO(s)+4 NOX2(g)+OX2(g)\ce{2Cu(NO3)2(s) ->[\text{heat}] 2CuO(s) + 4NO2(g) + O2(g)}2Cu(NOX3​)X2​(s)heat​2CuO(s)+4NOX2​(g)+OX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 8

    One reactant → three products on heating → thermal decomposition.

  9. 9

    NOX2\ce{NO2}NOX2​ is an oxide of a non-metal; it dissolves in water to form an acidic solution → pH less than 7. (Acids and pH: Chapter 2.)

  10. Check: Cu 2 | 2; N 4 | 4; O 12 | 12 ✔.

  11. Answer (a) 2 Cu(NOX3)X2(s)→heat2 CuO(s)+4 NOX2(g)+OX2(g)\ce{2Cu(NO3)2(s) ->[\text{heat}] 2CuO(s) + 4NO2(g) + O2(g)}2Cu(NOX3​)X2​(s)heat​2CuO(s)+4NOX2​(g)+OX2​(g) (b) X = nitrogen dioxide, NOX2\ce{NO2}NOX2​ (c) thermal decomposition (d) pH below 7.

    Common trap: Leaving 12OX2\dfrac{1}{2}\ce{O2}21​OX2​ in the final answer instead of doubling everything.

E12●● StandardLong answer · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch1 LA 41

What happens when (a) zinc is added to copper sulphate solution, (b) aluminium is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, (c) silver is added to copper sulphate solution? Write equations where a reaction occurs.

Full solution

Given: three metal + solution pairs. Asked: what happens, with equations.

Concept used: a metal displaces a less reactive metal (or hydrogen) from its compound (Topic 6). Why it applies: each case is a free metal in a solution.

  1. 1

    (a)

    Zinc is above copper → zinc displaces copper.

  2. 2

    Reddish-brown copper deposits; the blue solution becomes colourless (zinc sulphate is colourless).

    Zn(s)+CuSOX4(aq)→ZnSOX4(aq)+Cu(s)\ce{Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)}Zn(s)+CuSOX4​(aq)​ZnSOX4​(aq)+Cu(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 1

    (b)

    Aluminium is above hydrogen → it displaces hydrogen; bubbles of hydrogen form.

  4. 2

    Chlorine: 1 on the left, 3 in AlClX3\ce{AlCl3}AlClX3​ → try 3 HCl; hydrogen then 3 (odd) → double: 6 HCl.

  5. 3

    6 H → 3 HX2\ce{H2}HX2​; 6 Cl → 2 AlClX3\ce{AlCl3}AlClX3​; 2 Al.

    2 Al(s)+6 HCl(aq)→2 AlClX3(aq)+3 HX2(g)\ce{2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) -> 2AlCl3(aq) + 3H2(g)}2Al(s)+6HCl(aq)​2AlClX3​(aq)+3HX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 1

    (c)

    Silver is below copper → it cannot displace copper → no reaction.

  7. Check: (a) all elements 1 | 1, O 4 | 4; (b) Al 2 | 2, H 6 | 6, Cl 6 | 6 ✔.

  8. Answer (a) copper deposits, blue fades (equation above) (b) hydrogen bubbles (equation above) (c) no reaction.

    Common trap: In (b), writing Al+3 HCl→AlClX3+HX2\ce{Al + 3HCl -> AlCl3 + H2}Al+3HCl​AlClX3​+HX2​ — hydrogen does not balance (3 | 2).
